opening_summary: Thirty-three terms for making motion in Godot, from clips and tracks to tweens, bones and headless checks. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent what to change, and test that it really happened.
opening_description: 33 terms: clips, tracks, tweens, bones, checks.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. A newcomer usually thinks an animation is something a node does by itself. It is not. An Animation is data, a length and tracks of keys, and nothing moves until an AnimationPlayer plays it. Many of the terms ahead come in pairs that are easy to mix up. This film takes them group by group, and shows each one at work.
idea.text:
An Animation is
something a node does.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-three terms about making motion in Godot, and checking that it happens when you think, in four groups. The first group is clips and players, the Animation resource, AnimationPlayer, AnimationLibrary and AnimatedSprite2D. It covers what holds the motion, and what plays it.

The second group is tracks and keys. Track, key, playhead and interpolation, then the value, method, Bezier and audio tracks. These terms say what a clip is made of, and how values are filled in between the stored points.

The third group is time and tweens. Loop mode, loop seam, speed scale, autoplay, the animation finished signal, callback modes, update mode, Tween, easing, transition type and kill. They say when things run, how fast, and how code drives motion.

The fourth group is bones and checks. Skeleton, rest pose, inverse kinematics, pole target, FABRIK, look-at, SkeletonIK3D, skeleton updated, fixed frame rate and backend limit. They cover posing a body, and what you can test headless, with no window.

A code box shows one clip, named attack fast. An Animation resource is stored animation data, a length plus tracks of keys. This one is zero point four five seconds long, with a rotation track and a method track among its four. It is data, not behaviour, so nothing moves until a player plays it. For example, a spinning coin in your game could be a single Animation resource with one rotation track, saved in the coin's scene file.

Now an AnimationPlayer is joined to that clip. The AnimationPlayer is the node that plays animations by name. It moves the playhead along the clip and the property follows, so at zero point four five seconds the blade's rotation is seventy-five degrees. The Animation is the data, and the AnimationPlayer is the node that plays it. For example, the Walker sword scene has its own AnimationPlayer node, and the sword script tells it which attack clip to play on each swing of the combo.

A box of five names is linked to one clip. An AnimationLibrary is a named collection of animations that a player holds. It maps each name to an Animation resource, and calling play with a name picks one. Here the name attack fast picks a clip zero point four five seconds long. For example, the Walker sword's AnimationPlayer holds five animations, among them idle, attack fast and attack medium, so the combo code only has to ask for a name.

Two ways to play a sprite sheet. An AnimatedSprite2D is a 2D node that plays a list of frames, and that is all it does. In this made-up example it shows four frames at eight frames per second, half a second per cycle. An AnimationPlayer can key the frame too, and also position and monitoring, on one timeline. For example, a coin that just flips through four drawings fits an AnimatedSprite2D, but an attack whose hitbox must switch on with a frame needs an AnimationPlayer.

An empty chart, labelled with one property, rotation degrees. A Track holds one property's keyframes inside a clip, bound to a node path. One track means one property on one node, and its keys will sit on this line, between zero and zero point four five seconds. For example, if your player's jump clip should both squash the sprite and lift it, that takes two tracks, one for its scale and one for its position.

Three red dots sit on the track. A Key is one point on a track, holding a time, a value and an easing value. This sword track has three, minus eighty degrees at zero, eighty-five degrees at zero point one five seconds, and seventy-five at zero point two. A key is a stored point, not the place the clip has reached. For example, a door in your level needs two keys on its rotation track, shut at the start and open at the end.

A red line sweeps across the track. The Playhead is the marker for the current time on the timeline. The engine looks up the track at that time and sets the property, so at zero point four five seconds the rotation is seventy-five degrees. Keys stay put, and the playhead moves. For example, when you drag along a clip's timeline in the Godot editor to check a jump pose, you are moving the playhead by hand.

Three lines now join the same keys. Interpolation is how the values between keys are filled in. Nearest takes the value of the closest key, linear draws a straight line, and cubic bends a smooth curve. At zero point zero six seconds they give minus eighty, minus fourteen and minus seventeen point five degrees. For example, a pixel-art arm that should snap from pose to pose wants nearest, while a camera that glides wants linear or cubic.

Four lanes run under one playhead. A Value track sets a property, such as rotation degrees, to the keyed value at each moment. The top lane is the sword's rotation, ending at seventy-five degrees. A value track sets a property, while a method track calls a function. For example, a spike trap in your level could switch its visible property on and off with a value track.

The second lane is a Method track. It calls a function at chosen times, here at zero point one zero seconds, to open the combo input buffer, and at zero point two five seconds, to allow the next swing. It does not fire when you scrub in the editor, only in a running game. For example, a door clip could call a function that unlocks the exit at the moment the door is fully open.

The third lane is a Bezier track. It fills a value in between keys along a curve you shape by hand in the editor, not along a fixed rule. In this made-up curve the value runs from zero up to one. For example, a camera that swoops into a boss room along a curve you have dragged into exactly the shape you want would use a Bezier track.

The bottom lane is an Audio track. It plays a sound stream at a chosen time in the clip. In this made-up example a whoosh starts at zero point one zero seconds and is still playing. For example, a sword attack in your game could carry its swing sound on an audio track, so the sound is timed by the clip itself and not by a separate script.

Three graphs show where the playhead sits over six seconds, for a clip two seconds long. Loop mode is the setting for whether a clip plays once, loops, or ping-pongs. At six seconds the play-once clip has stopped at its end, the loop is back at zero, and the ping-pong is at its end again. Loop wraps from end to start, and ping-pong reverses at each end. For example, a walk cycle loops, while a death animation plays once.

Two loops of a walk-cycle angle. A Loop seam is a jump where the last value meets the first as a clip loops. In this made-up example the upper loop ends at minus ten degrees, so it jumps twenty degrees. The lower one ends at minus thirty, where it began, so no seam. To test it, compare the value at zero and at length. For example, a run cycle whose last frame differs from its first makes the character hitch once every loop.

Three bars race through one clip, zero point four five seconds long. Speed scale is a multiplier on how fast a clip plays, and the time to finish is the length divided by it. At a speed scale of zero point five the clip takes zero point nine seconds, and at two it takes zero point two two five. For example, a slow-motion power-up could set the player character's AnimationPlayer to a speed scale of zero point five, so attacks take twice as long.

Two bars on a timeline of seconds after a scene loads. Autoplay names the animation a player starts by itself when its scene loads. In this made-up example the top clip starts at zero seconds. Without autoplay, the lower clip waits for a script to call play, here at one point five seconds. For example, a torch flickering on a dungeon wall is a good autoplay clip, since it should run from the moment the level appears, with no code.

Now two clips end differently. Animation finished is the signal an AnimationPlayer sends when a clip ends. The clip that plays once sends it at its end. A looping clip never ends, so it never sends the signal. For example, your game over screen could wait for the death clip's animation finished signal, but if that clip were set to loop, the screen would never appear.

Callback modes set when animation updates, idle or physics, and when method keys run, deferred or immediate. Here a key at zero point one zero seconds, at one hundred twenty frames per second, falls on frame twelve on paper. Play leaves the playhead at zero on the first frame, and a deferred call waits for the frame to end, so on the Walker sword it was observed on frame fourteen. For example, a test asserting that your sword's method key fires on frame twelve would fail.

Two graphs of one value, keyed zero and then one at zero point one five seconds, in this made-up example. Update mode is set per value track. Continuous blends between keys, so the upper line climbs. Discrete changes only at the keys, so the lower line jumps. A yes-or-no value has nothing in between, so it wants discrete. For example, when the Walker sword's hitbox was moved into its attack clips, it went on a discrete monitoring track, true and then false.

Three lines climb from a camera zoom of one point zero. A Tween is a value animated from code toward a target, then thrown away. Its end value comes from gameplay, looked up at run time. The grey Animation always ends at two point zero, while Tween A ends at two point five and Tween B at one point eight, set by the player's target. For example, a health bar sliding down to whatever health the player has left is a tween.

Four balls make the same trip in one second. Easing is the speed curve of a change. Ease-in starts slow, and ease-out ends slow. At zero point two five seconds the linear ball is twenty-five percent of the way, ease-in six, ease-out forty-four, and ease-in-out thirteen. For example, a pause menu that moves in with ease-out moves quickly at first, then settles gently into place.

Six small graphs, each an ease-out curve. Transition type is the family of curve a tween follows, such as linear, sine, cubic, back, bounce or elastic. Easing says which end is slow, and the transition type says the shape. Back overshoots, reaching one point zero nine at the halfway mark, while bounce and elastic wobble to rest. For example, a coin that pops out of a block with the back type flies slightly past its spot before settling.

One sword tween runs to the end, and an identical one is stopped halfway. Kill a tween, and it aborts where it is, short of its end value, and its final step never runs. Killed at zero point zero seven five seconds, the blade stays at two point five degrees and the hitbox stays on. So a gameplay fact like an active hitbox belongs in an Animation. For example, a zoom tween killed when the player dies leaves the camera half zoomed.

A two-bone arm, an upper arm and a forearm. A Skeleton is a hierarchy of bones, where a child bone moves with its parent. Turn the upper arm to minus fifty degrees, and the forearm, set seventy degrees from it, rides along with the hand. Setting angles and then finding the hand like this is forward kinematics. For example, rotating only the thigh bone of a 2D character swings the shin and foot too, because they are its children.

A dashed straight arm appears beneath the bent one. The Rest pose is the skeleton's default pose, which you can return to at any time. Here every rest angle is zero, and the current pose sits minus fifty and seventy degrees away from it. Every animated pose is measured from rest. For example, an enemy whose arms are left bent after its attack clip can be reset to its rest pose before its next clip begins.

Now the hand chases a moving target. Inverse kinematics, or IK, means you choose the target, and the solver computes the joint angles that reach it. For two bones the law of cosines solves it. In this made-up arm the target is one hundred ninety-one from the shoulder, out of a reach of two hundred eighty, and the angle at the elbow is eighty-six degrees. For example, in the Walker IK build the mouse moves a target, and the robot's arms are solved to reach it.

Two elbows, one up and one down, both reach the same target. A Pole target is a helper point that sets which way an elbow or knee bends. Both solutions are correct, so only the pole can decide. Here the elbow goes down, the side nearer the pole. For example, a pole placed in front of a character's knee keeps the leg bending forward, never backwards.

A three-bone chain is pulled to a target, pass by pass. FABRIK, forward and backward reaching inverse kinematics, is an IK solver that moves the chain back from the target, then forward from the root, again and again until it fits. In this made-up chain the error falls from two hundred fifty-five pixels to nine point five after four passes. For example, the Walker IK build uses a FABRIK plugin written in GDScript to pull a robot's arms toward the target.

Both arms of a figure reach for one target. SkeletonIK3D is the older IK node built into Godot. Give it a bone chain and a target node, and it solves the chain for you. Its class reference marks it Deprecated, which means it may be changed or removed in a future version. For example, the Walker IK build runs SkeletonIK3D on both of the robot's arms, and its check confirms that the solver is running.

A single circle turns to face a target. Look-at rotates one bone so it faces a target. No chain is solved, only one angle, here minus twenty degrees. That is the difference from IK, which bends a whole chain. For example, a guard whose head bone turns to watch the player sneak past uses look-at, while reaching out with his arm would need IK.

Two readings of the same arm, taken at two moments. Skeleton updated is the signal a skeleton sends when its final pose, IK included, is ready to read. Sampled after a timer, the hand is still off the target, because the IK has not been applied yet. Sampled in the signal, it sits on the target. For example, the Walker IK test first sampled the arms after a timer and passed ten of twelve checks, then sampled them in this signal and passed all twelve.

Four rows of frame ticks, from a simulated run. A Fixed frame rate, set with the fixed fps flag and a number, makes every frame advance game time by exactly one over that number, in seconds. Pinned, the first frame at or past zero point one seconds is frame twelve every time. Unpinned, it drifts between twelve and thirteen. For example, the sword timing test written for Walker passed twenty of twenty pinned, and failed seven, nine and nine checks without the flag.

A mouse mode request, and a grid of eight checks. A Backend limit is something a headless run cannot test, such as a captured mouse, so it stays unverified, not passed. The Walker first-person scene asked for mouse mode two, captured, and got back zero, visible. So four of its eight navigation checks fail and stay unverified. For example, if your game hides the cursor for mouse look, report that as unverified until someone plays it in a real window.

Each pair puts two look-alike ideas side by side. An Animation is a clip with the end value in it, one point zero every time, and designers scrub it. A Tween is computed in code toward a target from gameplay, here zero point eight.

Loop wraps from the end straight back to the start, so the playhead jumps. Ping-pong plays forward, then backward, and repeats, so it never jumps. Only a loop needs its first and last values to match.

Two-bone IK is solved in one step with the law of cosines. FABRIK repeats, pass after pass, until the chain fits the target, here on pass four of four. Two bones get an exact answer at once, and a longer chain is solved by repeating.
Continuous blends between keys, so a value climbs smoothly from one key to the next. Discrete changes only at the keys, so it holds, then jumps. Use discrete for anything that is simply on or off.

Each vague request is turned into an exact instruction, beside a chart of what it does. Make the swing slower becomes, set speed scale to zero point five on attack fast. Zero point four five seconds becomes zero point nine. Half speed doubles the time.

Make the zoom feel smooth becomes, tween the zoom from one point zero to two point five over one second, with the quad transition type and ease-out. At zero point two five seconds the zoom is already one point six six, against one point three eight for linear.

Make the arm reach the target becomes, two-bone IK from shoulder to hand, with a pole target above the elbow. At a target distance of one hundred the elbow angle is forty-one degrees, and at two hundred seventy it is one hundred forty-nine. A farther target means a straighter elbow.

The hitbox should match the swing becomes, key monitoring true at zero seconds and false at zero point one five, with update mode discrete. On paper that is frames zero to eighteen at one hundred twenty frames per second. Observed, frames two to twenty. Check frames, not just seconds.

Test the animation headless becomes, run with the fixed fps flag at one hundred twenty, and read the pose in skeleton updated. Pinned, the timing test failed none of its twenty checks. Unpinned, the same test failed seven, nine and nine. Pin the time step first.

This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change to an animation. First, does a designer need to scrub it? Then it belongs in an Animation. Does gameplay set the end value? Then it is a Tween.
Second, if the clip loops, do its first and last values match, so there is no loop seam? And is the loop mode actually set?
Third, is every yes-or-no property, such as a hitbox's monitoring, keyed with update mode discrete, so it jumps at the key instead of blending?
Fourth, on which frame does the key really fire? The callback modes can move it, as the deferred call and the first frame after play did for the Walker sword.
Fifth, do you read the pose in the skeleton updated signal, once the final pose with IK is ready, and not after a timer, which can look between updates?
Sixth, did you pin the time step, and did you say what a headless run cannot test? Then say it exactly. Not make it smoother, but the quad transition, ease-out, one second.

recap_lines: An Animation is data, and an AnimationPlayer is the node that plays it.
A track binds one property, and its keys are the points it passes through.
A method track calls a function, and it never fires while you scrub.
A tween reads its end value from gameplay, and can be killed halfway.
Inverse kinematics sets the target and solves the angles, and a pole picks the bend.
Read the pose in skeleton updated, and pin the time step before you test.

your_turn.command: Give me short cases from making a game in Godot, one at a time, each showing an animation idea at work. Draw on AnimationPlayer, track, key, playhead, method track, update mode, loop seam, Tween, inverse kinematics and pole target. I answer with the exact term and say why its look-alike does not fit. Wait for my answer before you reveal yours.
checks: Check: every case comes from making a game, and waits for your answer.
Check: you named the exact term and ruled out its look-alike.

deck_problems: Slide 6 step 4 (update mode): the heading says 'READ AT 0.075 S', but the two readouts follow the playhead to 0.300 s, so the final picture shows 'at 0.300 s: 1.00' and 'at 0.300 s: 1' and never the 0.075 s comparison (0.50 against 0) that the heading promises. The narration does not mention 0.075 s.

Slide 6: the TELL THESE APART box (Immediate call vs Deferred call) belongs to callback modes only, but it is on screen from step 1 (Autoplay) and step 2 (animation_finished), where it does not apply.

Slide 10: the TELL THESE APART box sets 'Timer wait: reads between updates' against 'Fixed frame rate: reads on a known frame'. In Chapter 10 the timer problem in walker-3d-ik (reading the pose between skeleton updates, 10 of 12) was fixed by reading in skeleton_updated, not by a fixed frame rate, and the chapter says the existing create_timer waits pass at any frame rate but cannot pin a frame. The box joins two separate fixes; the natural partner of 'timer wait' is skeleton_updated.

Slide 12 step 5: the instruction is 'Run with --fixed-fps 120 and read the pose in skeleton_updated', but the chart (0, 7, 9 and 9 failed of 20) comes from the 2D sword timing test, which has no skeleton, so skeleton_updated played no part in those runs. The '0 of 20' to '9 of 20' labels also run over the chart's right border.

Badges understate real data: slide 6 is 'Illustrative data' though step 3 (key on paper frame 12, observed frame 14) is a Chapter 10 measurement, and slide 10 is 'Simulation (seeded)' though 10 of 12, requested 2 observed 0, 4 of 8, 20 of 20 and 7, 9, 9 are all real Chapter 10 results; only the frame ticks and the 139 px are simulated. The reverse holds on slides 4, 5, 8 and 9, badged 'Computed' while their notes call the Bezier curve, audio clip, walk-cycle values, bone lengths and chain lengths illustrative.

Slide 3 step 4: linear at 0.06 s is given as -14.0 degrees, a straight line between the first two keys, but the chapter prints a transition of 0.439427 on the first attack_fast key, so the real sword track would not read -14.0 there. The slide labels the track as the sword's.

Slide 8 step 3 and slide 12 step 3: 'elbow bends 86°' and 'elbow bend: 41° at reach 100, 149° at 270' give the interior angle at the elbow (law of cosines, 85.7 degrees for 191 of 280), so a straight arm would 'bend' 180 degrees. 'Bend' reads the opposite way; 'elbow angle' would be clearer. The narration says 'bends to' on slide 8 and 'elbow angle' on slide 12.
Slide 7 step 1 gives the Animation's fixed end value as 2.0, slide 11 pair 1 as 1.0, with the same picture idea; a viewer may take the two as a contradiction.

Layout: on slide 8 step 4 the lower elbow and its circle are drawn over the caption 'Both elbows reach the target'; on slides 6 and 7 step 4 the caption runs straight into the 'TELL THESE APART' label; on slide 5 step 3 the still ends with all three speed-scale bars full and equal, so the end picture does not show that 0.5 takes longer; slide 9 step 2 says 'both hands within 0.0 px of the target'.
